titre: Robert Merton and Science's Four Norms
accroche: In 1942, in the middle of a war against a “German science,” a sociologist set out four unwritten rules that distinguish science from ideology.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1942, Nazi Germany occupies a large part of Europe and proclaims the existence of a “German science,” purged of what the regime calls Jewish physics. It is in this climate that the American sociologist Robert K. Merton (1910-2003), of Columbia University, publishes a short article titled “Science and Technology in a Democratic Order.” It describes no discovery: it describes the unwritten rules that, in his view, hold together a community that truly does science, as opposed to a science placed in the service of a regime.

## Four Norms, Not Four Laws

Merton isolates four of them, later summarized by commentators under the acronym CUDOS. Communalism holds that any verified result belongs to the whole community, never to an individual who would keep it secret for personal gain: a researcher is entitled only to recognition for a discovery, not to its ownership. Universalism holds that the validity of a claim depends neither on the nationality, nor the religion, nor the social status of whoever states it, only on impersonal criteria, the same for everyone. Disinterestedness holds that the institution as a whole serves the advancement of shared knowledge, not the glory or gain of any one researcher. Organized skepticism, finally, holds that every claim must be submitted to critical scrutiny before being accepted, even one stated by an established authority.

Merton insists on one point: “The mores of science possess a methodological rationale but they are binding, not only because they are procedurally efficient, but because they are believed right and good.” These are not technical recipes, he says, but moral prescriptions: a researcher who fakes an experiment commits more than a methodological error, they violate a rule the community holds to be good in itself.

## What This Shifts

We often think science is distinguished from ideology by its method: experiment, measurement, proof. Merton shifts the question elsewhere. What protects a result from dogma is not merely a protocol, it is a social organization that makes cheating visible and costly. The Nazi regime offered, before his eyes, the living counter-example: a science whose validity depended on the race of whoever formulated it, the exact opposite of the universalism he describes.

But Merton's norms guarantee no behavior: they are ideals, not facts. Sociologists who came after him, including Ian Mitroff, have shown that very real counter-norms (secrecy, the stubborn defense of one's own theories, favoritism) coexist in practice with Merton's, without one erasing the other. A scientific community is therefore not a place where these four rules apply automatically: it is a place where their violation remains detectable, and can cost a reputation.

carte.punch: A scientific community is not defined by its method, but by four unwritten rules.
carte.idee: In 1942, facing a “German science” purged of its Jewish scholars, sociologist Robert Merton set out four unwritten norms (sharing, universalism, disinterestedness, organized skepticism) that distinguish genuine science from science placed in the service of an ideology.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Biography: born July 4, 1910 in Philadelphia, died February 23, 2003 in New York; career at Columbia University from 1941.

quiz.question: According to Robert Merton, what does the norm of “organized skepticism” consist of?
choix: Each researcher must first distrust their own results, before those of their colleagues
Every scientific claim must be submitted to critical scrutiny before being accepted, even one stated by an established authority
A result cannot be published before being reproduced in another laboratory
Judging a theory is reserved to the only specialists directly competent on the subject
quiz.explication: Organized skepticism demands systematic critical scrutiny of every claim, even one coming from an established authority; neither self-distrust, nor priority given to replication, nor reserving judgment to specialists alone defines this norm in Merton's account.
